segments.text:
Welcome to the back streets of the Opéra. Monumental Paris is never far away here. But on this walk, we're going to look beyond the grand façades, and discover what lies behind them.

Side streets. Buildings we pass without really noticing. Addresses that have belonged to photographers, collectors, soldiers and aristocrats.

Before we begin, take a moment to look around you.

We're about to follow the Rue Louis-le-Grand. It sounds like a thoroughly royal name, doesn't it? But the street hasn't always been called that. During the French Revolution, it became the Rue des Piques. A few years later, it was renamed Rue de la Place-Vendôme, before eventually recovering the name it bears today.

Even a street sign can conceal several different versions of Paris. And that's what we're here to discover: layer after layer.

We'll begin with a photographer whose pictures brought portraiture, justice, politics and visual manipulation into a surprisingly tangled relationship.

Just a few doors away, another address will lead us to a political assassination in December nineteen seventy-seven.

Then we'll enter the world of Joséphine, the Empress, and the remarkable possessions associated with Malmaison.

After that, the neighbourhood will change century almost without warning. We'll return to Paris during the Liberation, in August nineteen forty-four.

And finally, we'll travel much further back, to an aristocratic duel that ended with one of the men dead.

Five remarkable stories. But the walk between them matters, too.

Look at the façades. The corners of the streets. The upper floors. The sudden changes in scale. The little details that appear perfectly ordinary at first glance.

Because here, the small things can reveal just as much as the grand monuments.

Our first story begins with a man who understood, remarkably early, that a photograph could do much more than show someone's face.

Now, let's make our way to number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

segments.title: Ernest Appert — 21 Rue Louis-le-Grand
segments.text:
We've arrived at our first stop, at number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand. Take a good look at this address.

There is nothing here today to suggest that this building played a part in one of the more remarkable chapters of French photographic history.

Yet, in the second half of the nineteenth century, this address was associated with two brothers who took photography far beyond the conventional portrait.

And some of their pictures raise a question we're still asking today.

Can we believe what we see in a photograph?

To understand the brothers' story, we need to go back to the eighteen sixties.

In Paris, photography was becoming a business. Portraits were fashionable. People collected them in albums, exchanged them and gave them to family and friends.

But having your photograph taken was considerably more complicated than pulling a phone out of your pocket.

You had to visit a studio. The lighting had to be carefully controlled. The photographer prepared the plate, the chemicals and the backdrop. And the sitter needed to remain still long enough for a sharp image.

Every portrait called for real skill.

Two brothers worked in this world: Eugène Appert and Ernest-Charles Appert.

They came from Châteauroux, in central France. In Paris, they established themselves among professional photographers, including at this very address, number twenty-one Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Their speciality?

Important people.

Politicians, military officers, judges, aristocrats and public figures.

This was a world in which owning a photograph of a famous person was becoming a way of collecting the news.

Gradually, however, the brothers' work drew closer to something rather different: the world of criminal justice and political upheaval.

Before we come to that, I want to show you an extraordinary little piece of evidence.

A photographic card held by the Rijksmuseum, in Amsterdam, has a kind of advertisement printed on the back.

There are the photographer's professional titles. His claimed distinctions. His associations with prestigious figures.

And his address: number twenty-four, Rue Taitbout.

Then come two more words in French: “Ci-devant”.

Formerly.

The card tells us that the studio had previously been at number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Even after moving away, the photographer kept the old address on his printed cards.

And here you are, standing directly outside it.

It's a wonderful connection across time.

A tiny line of print, on the back of a photograph, allows us to identify a place that almost nobody would notice as they walked past, more than a hundred and fifty years later.

But what comes next is even more surprising.

The Appert brothers didn't simply photograph people sitting in front of studio backdrops.

They also used a technique that feels remarkably modern: photomontage.

Today, we're familiar with software that can remove a person, change a background or create an entirely imaginary scene.

By the late eighteen sixties, photographers could achieve some of these effects using painstaking manual techniques.

They could assemble portraits. Cut and combine photographic prints. Add drawings or painted details. And then photograph the composite image to create a new print.

Now look at this picture.

Several men appear to be gathered around a table. At first glance, it looks like a scene captured as it happened.

But it is a photomontage.

And that is where the technique becomes fascinating.

A photographer could create the appearance of a meeting that had never been photographed as a meeting.

He could bring different people together into a single composition.

And, crucially, he could lend that constructed scene the apparent authority of a photograph.

People in the nineteenth century did not necessarily have the habits of scepticism that we have developed towards manipulated images.

Then came eighteen seventy.

France went to war with Prussia. The Second Empire collapsed. And Paris approached one of the most violent periods in its history.

In eighteen seventy-one, the Paris Commune erupted. Civil conflict divided the city. There was terrible bloodshed. Hostages were executed. And the suppression of the Commune also cost very many lives.

The Apperts photographed people associated with these events.

But they also produced reconstructed scenes.

One series carried an arresting title: “The Crimes of the Commune”.

Among the events depicted were executions.

And here we need to make a vital distinction.

An event may really have happened.

But a photograph apparently showing that event may have been reconstructed afterwards.

The camera was not necessarily present when it happened.

The figures may have been photographed separately. The setting may have been assembled later.

And yet the finished picture can make you feel as though you're witnessing the very moment of the action.

Take the execution of hostages at La Roquette prison, in May eighteen seventy-one.

The event is part of the history of the Commune.

But Appert's picture is not a photograph taken during the execution.

It is a reconstruction.

And that distinction changes everything.

Imagine someone looking at such a photograph just weeks after the events.

They see a dramatic scene. Victims. Armed men. A setting that seems convincing.

They may believe they're looking at direct evidence.

But what they're looking at is an image composed by a photographer.

This takes us to one of the great questions in the history of the media.

A photograph can be a genuine photographic object, even when the scene it depicts was never photographed in that form.

And there's another dimension to all this.

These pictures circulated in a France deeply divided by politics.

They were not merely technical curiosities.

They could influence how people understood and remembered what had happened. They helped shape a narrative.

Photography was becoming more than a way to preserve history.

It could also be a way of interpreting history.

And sometimes, of steering that interpretation.

Now turn your attention back to the building in front of you.

It might seem that we've simply made an imaginary visit to a nineteenth-century Parisian photography studio.

But the story reaches much further.

At the very moment photography was coming to symbolise truth, some photographers were already learning how to create convincing pictures of reconstructed events.

And there's one final detail worth knowing.

The two brothers often worked under very similar commercial signatures. Archives and catalogues sometimes attribute their photographs differently.

So we must be careful when deciding exactly which work belongs to Eugène and which to Ernest-Charles.

What we can say is that their shared enterprise belongs to the earliest chapters of this extraordinary history of constructed photographic images.

Take one last look at number twenty-one, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

A small Parisian address.

And behind it, an enormous question.

When we look at an image from the past, are we seeing history itself?

Or are we seeing the way somebody chose to show it to us?

Keep that thought in mind.

Our next stop is only a short distance away. And it will take us to a much more recent event.

This time, it won't be a photograph that provides the clue.

It will be a gun.

Now, let's make our way to our second stop, further along Rue Louis-le-Grand, where we will uncover the story of Laïd Sebaï.

segments.title: From Ernest Appert to Laïd Sebaï
segments.text:
We haven't far to go.

But in those few steps, we're going to move forward almost a century.

Leave the nineteenth-century photography studios behind.

We're entering the Paris of the nineteen seventies.

The grand old façades are still standing.

But the life behind them has changed completely.

There are offices on the upper floors. Associations occupy other rooms. People arrive to work in the morning and leave again in the evening.

And some entrances still conceal courtyards and hallways that passers-by never see.

Look now at the large grey carriage doorway at number twenty-three.

Notice its two leaves, the carved decoration and the stone surround.

Building work here is documented in eighteen eighty-three and eighteen eighty-four.

We don't yet know exactly when the doors you can see were made.

But this entrance is an unmistakable landmark in the street.

In December nineteen seventy-seven, newspaper reports gave the address of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe as number twenty-three bis.

We cannot yet say with certainty which precise entrance that designation referred to.

The uncertainty about the doorway remains.

But the events themselves are coming into focus.

On the morning of Friday, the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven, a man was finishing his shift as a night watchman somewhere behind one of these entrances.

He was still inside the building.

The street was beginning to wake up.

He would soon be leaving.

But he would never make it home.

At the end of this short walk, we can finally give him his name.

Laïd Sebaï.

This is his story.

segments.title: Laïd Sebaï — The murder on Rue Louis-le-Grand
segments.text:
We've arrived at our second stop, on Rue Louis-le-Grand, at the site associated with the killing of Laïd Sebaï.

Look at this doorway.

Our story begins here, in July nineteen seventy-five.

During the night of the twenty-sixth to the twenty-seventh of July, sometime between two and half past two in the morning, much of Paris is asleep.

Then an explosion tears through the quiet outside the offices of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe, on Rue Louis-le-Grand.

A bomb has exploded outside the building.

The material damage here is relatively limited, and no casualties are reported.

But this is no isolated incident.

At almost the same moment, two more explosive devices strike premises belonging to the same organisation. One in Lyon. Another in Roubaix.

Three cities. Three buildings connected to the same organisation. And three explosions within a very short space of time.

In Lyon, the blast is powerful enough to shatter windows as far as eighty metres away. The damage in Roubaix is substantial too.

Here in Paris, the building at number twenty-three Rue Louis-le-Grand suffers less.

But the message is unmistakable. The Amicale des Algériens en Europe is being targeted in a coordinated series of bomb attacks.

In a statement, the organisation condemns another attack added to what it describes as a long sequence of violence.

Who planted the bombs?

Why attack three French cities at almost exactly the same time?

And who is trying to reach the organisation's leaders?

The first news reports do not clearly identify the perpetrators.

For now, remember one address. Number twenty-three, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Because a little more than two years later, another tragedy will unfold in the entrance hall of this building.

This time, the damage will not be confined to bricks and glass.

The months pass. Yet attacks against Algerian interests in France do not come to an end.

In the autumn of nineteen seventy-seven, tensions rise sharply.

On the fourth of November, an explosion strikes premises connected with Algerian interests near the Avenue de l'Opéra.

A few days later, more alarming news reaches the Algerian community.

On the fifteenth of November, the newspaper Le Monde publishes a disturbing report: two Algerians are said to have been abducted in Paris.

The story concerns an operation attributed to a group invoking the name Charles Martel, against a backdrop of tension over French citizens held by the Polisario Front.

The reported abduction appears in the press, but its exact date and circumstances are not completely established.

What matters is that the violence is no longer being described simply as damage to buildings. Men are now being reported as hostages.

Then comes the twenty-ninth of November.

Another explosion targets Algerian interests in the Opéra district.

We are now just three days away from the killing of Laïd Sebaï.

Look again at this entrance.

Two years earlier, a bomb had exploded outside these premises. Now fresh attacks are taking place nearby.

Threats and acts of violence are mounting.

We cannot establish that the same group was responsible for all these incidents.

But one thing is certain: when we reach the morning of the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven, the murder does not emerge from a peaceful background.

It follows a succession of attacks and alarms.

That Friday morning, Laïd Sebaï is finishing his shift.

He does not yet know that he will never go home.

It is Friday, the second of December, nineteen seventy-seven. Around half past nine in the morning.

Inside the Amicale's premises, a night watchman is coming to the end of his duty.

His name is Laïd Sebaï.

He is forty-six years old, and the father of seven children.

He is preparing to leave for home.

But armed men are waiting inside the building.

What happens next will make this address the scene of something far more tragic.

Because Laïd Sebaï is about to be murdered.

And there is a possibility that the killers have mistaken him for somebody else.

To understand why, we need to meet the man they may actually have intended to kill.

Abdelkrim Ghraieb.

At the time, Ghraieb is president of the Amicale des Algériens en Europe.

But that title tells us only part of his story.

During the Algerian War, he held positions of responsibility within the French federation of the National Liberation Front, or FLN.

After Algerian independence in nineteen sixty-two, the Amicale occupied an important place in relations between the Algerian authorities and the Algerian community living in France.

Ghraieb had connections and influence extending well beyond the walls of this street.

According to several historical accounts, the organisation's president and its night watchman bore a degree of physical resemblance, including a similar build.

And that resemblance may have cost Sebaï his life.

Let's return to the scene of the crime, while keeping two different accounts carefully apart.

The newspaper Rouge, reporting the following day, places the shooting in the entrance hall.

Sebaï is struck by several bullets and dies inside the building.

The paper says that after he falls, two Amicale employees who have just entered the lift to reach their offices are also fired upon.

The bullets miss them.

A later historical account describes a different sequence of movements. In that version, Sebaï had come downstairs with two people who took refuge in the lift.

So the sources do not entirely agree.

We have not found a reliable identification of those two survivors.

And we have no proof that Ghraieb was one of them.

Was Laïd Sebaï the intended target?

The possibility that he was mistaken for Abdelkrim Ghraieb appears very early in press coverage.

If the theory is correct, the gunmen killed the watchman while looking for an influential official of the organisation.

But we must not turn a hypothesis into a judicial finding.

We know armed men opened fire, and that Sebaï died.

We also know that, according to the contemporary newspaper account, other employees were shot at.

What we do not know with certainty is what the gunmen had in mind.

Very soon afterwards, an anonymous caller claims responsibility for the murder in the name of Delta.

That name recalls the commando units associated with the Secret Army Organisation, the OAS, during the Algerian War.

Fifteen years after Algerian independence, the choice of name carries a powerful meaning.

But a claim of responsibility is not a verified signature.

The callers say they are acting in retaliation for the detention of French citizens by the Polisario Front in Mauritania.

They threaten further violence against Algerians living in France.

The Algerian ambassador, Mohammed Bedjaoui, condemns the threats.

Trade unions, associations and political organisations protest.

Laïd Sebaï's body is repatriated to Algeria, where he is buried in the martyrs' section of El Alia cemetery.

For his family, the questions go far beyond the anonymous claims. Seven children have lost their father.

But the story does not end there.

On the fourth of May, nineteen seventy-eight, in the fifth arrondissement, another man is murdered near the lift of his building, at number four Rue Rollin.

His name is Henri Curiel.

He was on his way to a yoga class.

Curiel was born in Egypt. A communist activist and later an internationalist, he had helped networks supporting the Algerian National Liberation Front during the Algerian War.

Afterwards, he became involved with several anti-colonial movements.

He also worked to encourage contacts between Israelis and Palestinians.

His activities brought hostility and surveillance.

According to several contemporary sources, two armed men were waiting for him.

Curiel is killed.

Once again, the name Delta appears in a claim of responsibility.

The similarities are troubling.

Two murders in Paris. Two men connected in different ways to the history of Algerian independence. Attacks near lifts. And the same name appearing in claims of responsibility.

But similarities are not proof.

For that, we have to turn to ballistics.

On the twelfth of May, nineteen seventy-eight, Le Monde reports that one of the pistols used against Sebaï, a weapon of eleven point four three millimetre calibre, was also used in Curiel's murder.

The same gun.

Five months apart.

This time, the connection is physical evidence.

Yet the ballistic match does not identify the gunman, or the person who ordered either killing.

Investigators try to understand which organisations and networks might have been involved.

Former OAS militants, possible clandestine political networks, and possible links to intelligence services all become subjects of investigation.

The investigating judge, Guy Joly, encounters difficulties obtaining certain documents and securing interviews.

Questions surrounding the case persist for decades.

In his own account of events, the former police commissioner Lucien Aimé-Blanc implicates Jean-Pierre Maïone-Libaude.

Later, René Resciniti de Says claims, in testimony made public after his death, that he took part in the murder of Curiel.

He names Pierre Debizet, a leader of the Service d'action civique, as the alleged person who ordered it.

These are not judicial convictions.

Resciniti's account, including his claim about the supposed origin of a weapon, requires independent verification.

In October twenty twenty, a former inspector with France's domestic intelligence service, Marc Ducarre, is detained for questioning in the Curiel investigation.

He is released without prosecution at the end of that period of custody.

The names emerging from the case do not, by themselves, solve the murder.

Yet the investigation remains active.

In twenty twenty-five, magistrate Emmanuelle Ducos, working at the national unit for serial or unresolved crimes in Nanterre, requests the declassification of documents relating to the Curiel case.

In February twenty twenty-six, the French official gazette publishes another favourable opinion concerning the release of a series of notes and records.

That is not a verdict.

Nor is it proof that those archives contain the answer.

It tells us that investigators are still seeking to compare once-protected information with the rest of the evidence.

Now let us return to the man whose name began this story.

Look again at this doorway.

In July nineteen seventy-five, a bomb had already exploded outside the Amicale's premises.

In November nineteen seventy-seven, Algerian interests in Paris faced renewed attacks.

And then Laïd Sebaï was murdered at the end of his night shift.

Perhaps he was mistaken for the Amicale's president, Abdelkrim Ghraieb.

Ghraieb survived. He continued his career and became Algeria's ambassador to Iran, taking part in diplomacy surrounding the release of the American hostages in January nineteen eighty-one.

The contrast is striking.

The man who may have been the target went on to an international career.

The man who died left behind seven children.

Then a single gun created a material link between Sebaï's killing and the murder of Henri Curiel.

Almost half a century later, secret documents are still the subject of judicial requests.

We do not know whether those responsible for the bombings in nineteen seventy-five, the attacks in November nineteen seventy-seven and the murders belonged to the same networks.

We know the events followed one another.

We know one weapon was used in two killings.

And we know the possibility of mistaken identity has existed since the earliest stages of the investigation.

Why did Laïd Sebaï die that morning?

We can tell you what the historical records establish.

We cannot close the case on behalf of the investigators.

Now we leave the nineteen seventies behind.

Just a few steps away, another story awaits us, among the extraordinary collections of Joséphine de Beauharnais.

Now, let's make our way to number sixteen, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

In a few steps, we leave the political violence of the twentieth century and return to Joséphine and the dispersal of the collections at Malmaison. As you walk, remember that in Paris, an address can outlive its occupants, its purpose, and even the building that once stood there. In eighteen nineteen, number sixteen was the setting for an extraordinary sale.

segments.title: Joséphine and the dispersal of Malmaison
segments.text:
We've arrived at our third stop, at number sixteen, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Today, passers-by see just another address in the Opéra district.

But in March eighteen nineteen, this place brought several worlds together: the vanished French Empire, the world of science, faraway voyages and the collectors of Paris.

There was an auction here.

And the objects offered for sale came from Malmaison.

To understand how they arrived in this street, we need to meet the woman who had brought them together.

Joséphine de Beauharnais.

She had shared the rise of Napoleon Bonaparte, become Empress of the French, and then been divorced when Napoleon sought to secure the imperial succession.

Yet the Château de Malmaison, near Paris, remained her own particular world.

It was much more than an elegant home.

Over the years, she had turned it into a meeting place for gardens, works of art, curiosities, plants and rare animals.

Joséphine had a particular passion for botany.

She supported horticultural projects and collected plants brought from distant parts of the world.

In an age of major scientific expeditions, owning an unfamiliar plant or an object brought back from a voyage could reveal several things at once: a collector's curiosity, the ambitions of the state, and the networks of power that made such acquisitions possible.

But Joséphine died on the twenty-ninth of May, eighteen fourteen, shortly after Napoleon's first abdication.

She would never see his brief return to power in eighteen fifteen, or the Empire's second fall.

France changed its government.

Properties changed hands.

But fortunes, and debts, did not simply disappear.

Her son, Eugène de Beauharnais, inherited a substantial part of his mother's property.

There were financial obligations to settle as part of the estate.

And some of the collections were put up for sale.

This is where our little Parisian street enters the story.

The catalogue announced an auction originally due to begin on the fifteenth of March, eighteen nineteen.

It was postponed to the twenty-fourth.

And before the auctioneer's hammer began to fall, there were to be days when prospective buyers could inspect the objects.

Imagine the scene.

There's no need to invent the actions of any particular visitor.

People enter to examine the lots.

Some recognise the artists' names.

Others assess the material, the rarity, or the provenance of an object.

A dealer might consider its resale value.

A collector of curiosities might be drawn to something unusual.

Another visitor might want a souvenir of Malmaison.

The same object could mean entirely different things to different people.

Now, let's open the catalogue.

This isn't an ordinary household furniture sale.

There are sculptures and statues.

Vases. Tables. Marble objects. Engraved stones. Mosaics. Decorative pieces.

And then, gradually, the list takes a rather unexpected turn.

Minerals.

Shells.

Preserved birds.

Weapons and clothing from regions far beyond Europe.

And even objects described as mummies.

Mummies.

Offered at an auction on Rue Louis-le-Grand, in the spring of eighteen nineteen.

That word makes us stop and think today.

In historical classifications, it could refer to human remains. And that immediately raises questions about provenance, and about the treatment of the dead.

But nineteenth-century catalogues don't always tell us everything we would like to know.

Where, exactly, did these objects come from?

Who collected them?

Under what circumstances?

Through whose hands did they pass before reaching Malmaison?

An auction catalogue describes what is for sale.

It does not necessarily reconstruct an object's entire history.

That distinction is essential.

Some of these curiosities point towards the great era of European exploration in the early nineteenth century.

The catalogue connects certain pieces with the expedition led by the navigator Nicolas Baudin, who set out for southern waters in the early eighteen hundreds.

That scientific undertaking explored parts of the Australian coastline and brought many observations and collections back to Europe.

For Joséphine, the connections between major expeditions, scientists and the collections at Malmaison were particularly important.

But we cannot simply assign every item in the catalogue to a particular ship, collector or port of call.

The history of an object depends on evidence of its provenance.

Even so, think about the possible journey of some of these pieces.

From a coastline on the other side of the world.

Onto a ship, and then into a French port.

From a scientific collection into the rooms of Malmaison.

And, years later, to number sixteen, Rue Louis-le-Grand.

Something that may once have represented an extraordinary discovery becomes a numbered auction lot.

It is examined.

Valued.

Sold.

And carried away to another collection.

The sale also brought several periods of history together.

Among the objects were works and sculptures associated with the court of Louis the Sixteenth.

Some were linked to the Queen's Dairy at Rambouillet, a decorative complex created in the world of Marie Antoinette.

What a remarkable meeting of destinies.

Objects from a royal court overturned by the Revolution.

The collection of Joséphine, a former empress.

And then an auction in eighteen nineteen, under the restored monarchy.

In only a few decades, political power had changed hands again and again.

But objects could survive the fall of regimes.

Perhaps that's what makes this story so unusual.

At Malmaison, the collections had formed a whole.

There were books, gardens, a cabinet of curiosities, ceremonial rooms and personal souvenirs.

Together, they reflected the taste of a woman, her position in society and the age in which she lived.

But an auction breaks up that unity.

Things assembled over many years can be scattered in just a few sale sessions.

One sculpture goes to a house.

A vase is bought by an enthusiast.

A scientific curiosity passes into someone else's collection.

Sometimes an object's later journey can be traced through inventories, annotated catalogues and museum archives.

Others become difficult to follow.

The catalogue of eighteen nineteen is rather like a snapshot of a world at the precise moment it comes apart.

Look again at number sixteen.

The façade you can see today is later than the auction. It would be wrong to pretend we can identify the actual room where the sale took place.

But the address allows us to place the episode in the city.

Here, for a few days, the collections of Malmaison met the dealers and collectors of Paris.

We could tell Joséphine's story entirely through palaces, portraits and the grand ceremonies of the Empire.

But this place gives us another way to meet her.

Through the things left behind after her death.

Through the objects her heirs had to part with.

And through the traces preserved in old catalogues.

On one side, a woman who had sought to bring together the beauties and curiosities of the world.

On the other, an auction room where that collection becomes a succession of separate lots.

And between the two, only five years since her death.

A life doesn't disappear entirely when a person dies.

Books, furniture and treasured objects continue to travel.

But once separated, they no longer tell quite the same story.

Our next stop will take us to a building every bit as famous as Malmaison, but we'll see it under radically different circumstances.

The Palais Garnier.

And Paris, in August nineteen forty-four.

Now, let's make our way to the Palais Garnier.

This time, take your time.

As the street opens out, the neighbourhood begins to change scale. The views become longer. The buildings become grander. And soon, the Palais Garnier starts to dominate the scene.

But there is something easy to forget. This magnificent vista has not always existed.

In the middle of the nineteenth century, the Paris you are walking through was much more tightly packed.

The new opera house was being built, but the great avenue intended to connect it with central Paris had yet to be opened all the way through.

Entire blocks had to vanish. Streets were cut through. Houses were demolished.

During the eighteen seventies, the photographer Charles Marville recorded that transformation. Among other things, he photographed the opening of the avenue between Rue Louis-le-Grand and Rue d'Antin.

In other words, almost exactly where you are walking now.

Try, for a moment, to remove the avenue from the view in front of you.

Imagine a much denser network of narrow streets. Building sites. Façades sliced open. Plots of land covered with demolition rubble.

That great straight road, which seems so natural today, had to be created.

Keep walking.

Now, we're changing periods once again. It is August, nineteen forty-four.

Paris is rising against the German occupation. Barricades appear. Police officers and members of the Resistance take action.

Across a city now in revolt, German positions come under growing pressure.

One of those positions lies directly ahead of you: the German command post near the Opéra, known as the Platzkommandantur.

The Place de l'Opéra and Rue du Quatre-Septembre bring us back to these events.

segments.title: The German command post at the Opéra in 1944
segments.text:
We've arrived at our fourth stop, in front of the Palais Garnier.

Look towards the Palais Garnier.

Take a moment to study its façade.

The monumental steps. The statues. The columns. The grand perspectives.

This building was designed to impress.

It evokes glittering opera nights, elegant sets, bright lights and fashionable society.

But in August nineteen forty-four, the square in front of you was anything but a gala scene.

German soldiers still occupied positions in the French capital.

Paris was in revolt.

And a German military command post in the Opéra district became one of the flashpoints of those days.

Let's return to the nineteenth of August, nineteen forty-four.

After four years of occupation, events were moving quickly.

Police officers, Resistance fighters and armed groups were trying to regain control of different neighbourhoods.

But German forces were still present.

Paris had not yet been liberated.

Communications were difficult.

And the danger could change from one street to the next.

Photographs taken around the Opéra still show German soldiers, vehicles and military positions.

They're invaluable records.

We don't need to invent a vanished Paris.

We can see uniformed figures standing outside buildings that are still recognisable today.

Compare a window.

The corner of a façade.

The line of an avenue.

The same neighbourhood.

But a very different world.

The following day, the twentieth of August, those tensions lead to a death.

Two French police officers are in the area.

Their names are Michel Guillois and Pierre Gormond.

Guillois is helping deliver an order or message concerning a ceasefire.

The situation is confused.

In insurgent Paris, several efforts to arrange truces or agreements are intended to prevent further fighting.

But none of them makes every German position safe.

Gunfire breaks out near the command post.

According to a family account of the episode, a German officer ordered a sentry on a balcony to fire towards the police officers' vehicle.

That particular detail, about the order and the person who gave it, comes from the family testimony.

We must not present it as an independently established finding.

Michel Guillois is hit.

He dies.

According to the same preserved account, Pierre Gormond is wounded in the leg by two bullets.

This is five days before the Liberation of Paris.

Look up at the windows around you.

For the policemen moving through these streets, the grand architecture offered no special protection.

A German position could still open fire.

An ordinary journey along a familiar road could be fatal.

That's why it would be misleading to tell only the story of the command post's capture on the twenty-fifth of August.

The final assault was preceded by days of fighting, uncertainty and casualties.

The Palais Garnier was drawn into the war well before French armoured vehicles arrived.

Now let's move forward a few days.

On the evening of the twenty-fourth of August, advance elements of the Second French Armoured Division, under General Philippe Leclerc, entered Paris.

On the twenty-fifth, more units moved through the capital.

Resistance fighters, insurgent police and French soldiers began retaking different positions.

But German forces did not vanish all at once.

Each remaining strongpoint could require its own operation.

The Opéra district was one of them.

It's now the twenty-fifth of August.

In the middle of the afternoon, French troops attack the German command post.

Among those taking part is the Eleventh Company of the Third Battalion of the Régiment de marche du Tchad.

It's a rather technical name.

But this regiment was among the formations accompanying the Second Armoured Division on its advance.

The soldiers who arrived here had already endured long campaigns before reaching central Paris.

And an extraordinary historical photograph documents their action.

In the image, you can see a French half-track.

That's a vehicle with wheels at the front and tracks at the back.

It's towing a fifty-seven-millimetre anti-tank gun.

And painted on its side is an extraordinary name.

La Revanche, thirty-nine, forty.

La Revanche, thirty-nine, forty.

The Revenge.

A name painted on a military vehicle, but also a striking reminder of the journey since France's defeat in nineteen forty.

Four years earlier, the French army had collapsed before the German offensive.

Now French soldiers were helping to liberate their capital.

The vehicle's name cannot tell us what every man aboard was thinking.

But it does tell us what the vehicle was called.

And the inscription is visible in the photographic record.

Look again at the avenue as it appears today.

In the picture from nineteen forty-four, dark smoke obscures part of the view.

Ordinary shops and façades stand behind the military vehicles.

Those details matter.

The fighting is taking place in a living neighbourhood.

Not on some isolated battlefield.

A shopfront.

An apartment window.

A carriage entrance.

Completely ordinary features, suddenly caught up in a military operation.

We cannot make people in a photograph speak.

We don't know precisely what each soldier could see beyond the edge of the frame.

But we can identify vehicles, markings, buildings and the documented sequence of events.

That's already a great deal.

And it's how photographs can help us understand history without inventing it.

The French forces advance on the position.

The situation changes.

And then comes the surrender.

In another historical photograph, German servicemen are emerging, with a white flag visible.

French soldiers, Resistance fighters and civilians are gathered around them.

Only a short while earlier, the men holding this position had still been an armed occupying force.

Now they are becoming prisoners.

But let's be precise about what the pictures can establish.

A photograph can show people coming out, uniforms, a white flag and the crowd around them.

It cannot, by itself, reconstruct the entire surrender negotiation or every tactical movement that came before.

The twenty-fifth of August, nineteen forty-four, is remembered as the day Paris was liberated.

That's an accurate description of the wider historical event.

But it can obscure what came before.

The policeman killed on the twentieth.

His wounded colleague.

The last defended positions.

The men still advancing through the streets, unsure what waited around the next corner.

Liberation wasn't a single instant.

It was a succession of fights, orders, surrenders and risks, lived through by different people.

Take a few seconds to look at the Opéra.

Its architecture seems designed to last.

It had survived the fall of the Second Empire, under which construction first began.

It witnessed changes throughout the neighbourhood.

Then the Occupation.

And finally those days of August nineteen forty-four.

There's one last thing to do here.

Look at the historical photograph on your screen and try to place the camera in the real space around you.

Find the line of a cornice.

The position of a statue.

A street corner.

The outline of the Palais Garnier.

You're not watching a reconstruction with actors.

You're looking at an authentic archive, returned to the place where it makes sense.

And suddenly, the distance between nineteen forty-four and today seems a little shorter.

We're now going to travel much further back.

In our imaginations, the opera house will disappear.

So will the wide avenues.

Because our final stop takes place in sixteen fifty-two, when Paris was torn apart by the Fronde.

And when two brothers-in-law decided to settle a quarrel with weapons.

Now, let's make our way to our fifth and final stop, at the site of the former horse market behind the Hôtel de Vendôme.

segments.text:
For the next few minutes, try to forget almost everything you can see around you.

The Palais Garnier disappears. The Avenue de l'Opéra disappears. The grand nineteenth-century buildings disappear.

Even several of the streets cease to exist in anything like their present form.

We are travelling back to sixteen fifty-two.

And Paris is not merely different in its architecture. The kingdom itself is in crisis.

Louis the Fourteenth is only thirteen years old. The Fronde is tearing France apart.

Princes. Great families. Parliament. Armies. Rival factions.

Alliances change. People negotiate, betray one another, make peace, and sometimes reach for their weapons.

As you walk, look at the oldest buildings that have survived in this part of Paris.

They seem old enough to us. Yet even they were built after the world we are about to enter.

Nearby once stood the great Hôtel de Vendôme.

Behind it stretched a much more open space than anything you see here today: a horse market.

Replace the façades in your imagination with rough, uneven ground, crowded with horses and traders, dust in the air and voices calling out during the busy hours of the day.

On the evening of the thirtieth of July, sixteen fifty-two, this place becomes the setting for an armed encounter.

Not to buy a horse. To fight.

Two men arrive here.

François de Vendôme, Duke of Beaufort.

And his brother-in-law, Charles-Amédée of Savoy, Duke of Nemours.

They belong to the same political camp. They belong to the same family.

And yet, just a few minutes later, one of them will be dead.

segments.title: Beaufort and Nemours, the duel of 1652
segments.text:
We've arrived at our fifth and final stop, at the site of the former horse market.

Take a look around you.

Buildings. Shops. Streets full of cars and pedestrians.

It's hard to imagine that, right here in the middle of the seventeenth century, there was a horse market.

An open space behind the walls of the great Hôtel de Vendôme.

Men brought horses here, bargained over prices, and moved through a neighbourhood very different from the one you know today.

But on the thirtieth of July, sixteen fifty-two, this market became the scene of something Paris would talk about for years.

Ten men were going to fight here.

Two were princes.

They belonged to the same political faction.

They were even brothers-in-law.

And one would not leave alive.

To understand how a family quarrel became a deadly confrontation, we need to return to a deeply divided Paris.

It's sixteen fifty-two.

Louis the Fourteenth is only thirteen.

He has been king since he was four, but France is passing through a period of extraordinary political and military violence.

That period has a name: the Fronde.

For years, powerful nobles, magistrates and opposing groups have challenged royal authority, particularly the influence of Cardinal Mazarin.

Alliances change.

Armies move.

Some princes proclaim their loyalty to the king while fighting the forces defending his government.

By the summer of sixteen fifty-two, Paris is one of the main prizes in the conflict.

And even among Mazarin's opponents, rivalries can be ferocious.

That is the world inhabited by the two men in our story.

The first is François de Vendôme, Duke of Beaufort.

He is a grandson of Henry the Fourth.

That makes him a member of a prestigious branch of the royal family.

In Paris, Beaufort enjoys immense popularity among parts of the population.

He has even acquired a revealing nickname: the King of the Markets.

It is not an official title.

It reflects his reputation as a prince able to win popular support, especially in the capital's trading districts.

Beaufort commands men.

He intervenes in Parisian politics.

And his influence matters to the competing factions of the Fronde.

But he is not the only man with military authority.

Our second figure is Charles-Amédée of Savoy, Duke of Nemours.

He is younger than Beaufort.

A prince of the House of Savoy, he too is engaged in the military operations of the Fronde.

The two men know each other intimately.

And there is a very simple reason.

Nemours married Élisabeth de Vendôme, Beaufort's sister.

They are brothers-in-law.

Imagine their position.

Two great noblemen.

Two military commanders.

Two men from the same family circle.

And yet their relationship is becoming dangerously bitter.

This is not simply an argument over an inheritance or a private disagreement.

Their ambitions, their places in the chain of command and disputes about precedence are all creating friction.

In the aristocratic world of the seventeenth century, precedence is much more than a question of manners.

Who takes priority.

Who commands.

Who is expected to give way.

These things touch honour and power directly.

And when both men have armed supporters, an argument over rank can turn very serious indeed.

We have an extraordinary source for the final days before the duel.

The memoirs of Anne-Marie-Louise d'Orléans, Duchess of Montpensier, known to history as the Grande Mademoiselle.

A cousin of Louis the Fourteenth, she is at the centre of the Fronde.

She knows both men and the people close to them.

And she personally tries to prevent their quarrel from ending in disaster.

Her memoirs are not a sworn statement from someone who witnessed the duel.

But they help us reconstruct warnings, conversations and attempts to intervene before the encounter.

Earlier in July, Beaufort and Nemours had seemed to grow closer.

They had recently been caught up in fighting around the Faubourg Saint-Antoine.

On the second of July, the forces of the Prince of Condé clashed with royal troops at the gates of Paris.

Nemours was wounded.

Despite their disagreements, the two brothers-in-law then showed signs of friendship.

For Élisabeth de Vendôme, wife of one and sister of the other, the apparent reconciliation was a relief.

But it did not last.

A fresh dispute broke out about rank.

The Grande Mademoiselle reports that Beaufort appeared relatively conciliatory, while Nemours reacted with much greater anger.

Tensions grew so serious that the faction's principal leaders tried to intervene.

The Duke of Orléans and the Prince of Condé obtained a promise from Nemours.

For twenty-four hours, he would not challenge Beaufort.

They thought they had bought time.

Perhaps they could prevent the worst.

But warnings soon began to circulate.

The Grande Mademoiselle learned that Beaufort was walking in the Tuileries gardens.

He was not alone.

Several noblemen accompanied him.

She sent people to find out what was happening.

The Duchess of Nemours, equally anxious, tried to alert those around them.

Then came a message.

The two princes were apparently about to fight.

The Grande Mademoiselle hurried to warn the Duke of Orléans.

This time, there could be no doubt about the danger.

Men were sent to stop the meeting.

But they arrived too late.

Meanwhile, Nemours had decided to pursue the quarrel.

According to the account preserved by the Grande Mademoiselle, Beaufort tried to avoid the confrontation.

He pointed out that several gentlemen were with him.

The encounter should be postponed.

But Nemours would not be dissuaded.

If Beaufort had men with him, Nemours would fetch the same number.

What began as a quarrel between two people was becoming a group duel.

Five against five.

And this brings us back to where you're standing.

The horse market behind the Hôtel de Vendôme.

Late that afternoon, on the thirtieth of July, sixteen fifty-two, the two groups faced each other.

Historical accounts generally place the encounter at around seven in the evening.

Four gentlemen stood with Beaufort.

The Count of Bury.

The Count of Ris.

Brillet.

And Héricourt.

Opposite them, Nemours was accompanied by the Marquis of Villars, the Chevalier de La Chaire, Campan and Uzerche.

Some of their names appear with slightly different spellings in old accounts.

Ten men.

All armed.

And what the Grande Mademoiselle says about the weapons deserves particular attention.

The pistols and swords were apparently brought by Nemours.

The pistols, she reports, had been loaded at his home.

That detail matters because it shows how carefully the encounter had been prepared.

This was not a spontaneous scuffle between passers-by.

These men had brought weapons.

They had chosen a place.

They had arrived with companions.

And they knew they might die.

Then came an extraordinary moment.

According to the Grande Mademoiselle, Beaufort made one final attempt at reconciliation.

He addressed Nemours as a brother.

He suggested putting their quarrel behind them.

Becoming friends again.

Perhaps it was the last chance to prevent catastrophe.

But Nemours refused.

In the version passed down by the memoirist, he insisted that one of them must kill the other.

Nemours fired first.

His shot missed Beaufort.

A moment of silence.

Then Nemours advanced with his sword.

Beaufort answered with his pistol.

According to the testimony reported by the Grande Mademoiselle, the weapon had been loaded with three bullets.

A shot rang out.

Nemours was hit.

He staggered, fell, and died almost immediately.

Around them, the fighting continued.

The companions fought one another.

The Count of Bury was seriously wounded.

According to Voltaire's account, Héricourt fell to the Marquis of Villars.

And the Count of Ris also died of his wounds.

Within twenty-four hours, a dispute between brothers-in-law had cost three men their lives.

Three dead.

Including the Duke of Nemours.

And for once, the consequences were not merely political.

They were family consequences.

Terribly personal ones.

Nemours's wife was the sister of the man who had just killed him.

Élisabeth de Vendôme was about to learn that her husband had died at the hands of her own brother.

We should pause here over an important historical qualification.

Old accounts do not necessarily agree about every movement or exactly who fired which shot.

We know the outcome.

We know the main participants.

We know the location.

But the precision with which memoirists describe words and gestures does not mean they personally witnessed them.

The Grande Mademoiselle herself was passing on what she had been told about Nemours's last moments.

People rushed from the gardens of the Hôtel de Vendôme.

Among them was an abbess.

According to the account, she invoked Jesus and Mary.

Nemours was said to have squeezed her hand.

Was that a final conscious gesture?

The doctors and surgeons present were not convinced.

They believed the movement might have been a convulsion caused by his wounds.

This is the sort of detail history has preserved.

Not simply the death of a prince, but uncertainty over his last movement.

News began spreading through nearby streets.

And remarkably quickly.

The Grande Mademoiselle was still among the Duke of Orléans's circle when a servant from the Hôtel de Vendôme arrived.

The message was devastating.

Nemours was dead.

Beaufort had killed him.

The Duchess of Nemours learned of her husband's death almost immediately.

According to the memoirs, she heard cries in the courtyard.

She fainted.

Think what the news must have meant to her.

Her husband had just been killed.

And the man who killed him was her own brother.

Élisabeth found herself at the centre of a family tragedy whose tensions she had known and feared.

Nemours's death provoked another controversy.

His funeral.

At that time, duelling was not simply accepted by the Church.

Dying in such an encounter raised serious religious difficulties.

The Grande Mademoiselle reports that the Archbishop of Paris refused to allow public prayers for Nemours in his parish.

For his widow, it was another blow.

After losing her husband, she faced the spiritual and social consequences of the way he had died.

And what became of Beaufort?

He survived the encounter.

He remained an important figure in the closing years of the Fronde.

But his brother-in-law's death could not be undone.

Even those familiar with the affair argued over his responsibility.

Could he have avoided the confrontation?

Did he truly try to reconcile with Nemours until the very end?

Was he forced to defend himself?

The Grande Mademoiselle offers a version relatively favourable to Beaufort.

She emphasises his efforts to avoid the duel, and Nemours's aggression.

But remember, she was writing from within their family and political world.

Her account is invaluable.

It is not perfectly impartial.

And that is exactly what makes the case so fascinating to a historian.

We have names.

Dates.

A place.

Human consequences.

A detailed account of the preparations.

But we also have the perspective of a woman personally involved in these events, who knew the people concerned and tried to stop the confrontation.

It isn't a camera.

It's a memory.

A memory close to events, but shaped by the emotions and loyalties of its time.

Now return to the Paris around you.

The horse market disappeared long ago.

The Hôtel de Vendôme and its gardens no longer define this neighbourhood as they did in sixteen fifty-two.

The city has changed profoundly.

Old descriptions allow us to locate the area of the duel.

But it would be reckless to claim that we can point to the exact spot on today's pavement where Nemours fell.

Even so, we know what happened in this vicinity.

Two commanders from the same faction faced one another.

They were brothers-in-law.

People close to them tried to arrange a reconciliation.

Warnings circulated.

Men were sent to stop the fight.

And they arrived too late.

On the thirtieth of July, sixteen fifty-two, Paris witnessed more than the death of a prince.

It saw the divisions of the Fronde penetrate into the heart of a single family.

A man died at his brother-in-law's hands.

Other noblemen were killed or seriously wounded.

A wife lost her husband to her own brother.

And all this unfolded in a city already scarred by civil war.

Take one final look at these streets.

There are no horses gathered for market.

No garden walls enclosing the old Vendôme estate.

No armed noblemen awaiting their opponents.

Only the city remains.

And this story.

A meeting that several people had tried to prevent.

One last appeal for reconciliation.

And a few minutes in which aristocratic honour came at a terrible price.

This is the end of our final stop.

But before you leave the Opéra district, think back over the stories we've encountered.

Stories the façades can no longer tell.

And which the archives still allow us to recover.

Before you leave, take a few more seconds to look around you. You've travelled through several centuries without leaving a handful of streets. A photographer who understood how images can deceive. A night watchman murdered in nineteen seventy-seven. Joséphine's collections, dispersed piece by piece. A German command post attacked in the heart of Paris. And a deadly duel at a horse market that no longer exists. These stories seem to have little in common, yet they belong to the same small part of the city. Perhaps that's the most fascinating thing about Paris. Its different eras never disappear completely. They remain behind façades, beneath changed street names, beneath new avenues and beneath the everyday habits of the present. Sometimes all it takes is an address, a photograph, an old map or a forgotten story to bring those eras back into view. Now that you know these stories, you'll probably never see these streets in quite the same way again. And that is precisely what Velvet Passport is here to do. Not simply to show you Paris, but to help you discover how to read it. This is the end of your walk.
